title: Mural on the Stepped Wall
story: A school courtyard's old garden wall is built from columns of bricks, each one brick wide, side by side with no gaps. Some columns have lost bricks, so the top is a jagged staircase; a column of height 0 has none left.
The art class wants the biggest rectangular mural possible. It must sit on the ground, cover whole adjacent columns, and stay on bricks: no taller than the shortest column it spans.
task: Write largestMural(heights). heights[i] is the number of bricks in column i, each brick 1 × 1. Return the largest area, in bricks, of a rectangle spanning one or more consecutive columns and no taller than the shortest of them.
Return 0 for an empty wall or a wall with no bricks.

examples.explanation: Columns 0 to 2 (heights 3, 5, 4) are all at least 3 tall, so they give 3 × 3 = 9. The tallest column alone gives 6, columns 1 and 2 give 4 × 2 = 8, and any rectangle that includes column 3 is at most 1 tall, so it gives at most 1 × 6 = 6.
Columns 1 and 2 give 4 × 2 = 8. Column 3 has no bricks, so no rectangle can cross it, and the column of height 5 alone gives only 5.

hints: Fix one column, say the 4 in [3, 5, 4, 1, 6, 2], and make the mural exactly that tall. How far left and right can it stretch?

Every best mural is exactly as tall as its shortest column. So for each column, take the widest rectangle of its height: it stretches until a shorter column on each side. The answer is the best of these n candidates.
So each column needs its nearest shorter column on the left and on the right. That "next smaller" question is answered in one pass by a stack of columns with increasing heights.

Walk left to right with a stack of indexes whose heights increase. When column i is shorter than the top, pop the top: i is its right limit, and the new top (or -1 if empty) its left limit, so its area is height × (i - left - 1). Push i. At the end, add one extra column of height 0 to pop everything left.
bruteForce: Try every pair of start and end columns, keep a running minimum height as the end moves right, and compute minimum × width.
That is O(n²): about 5 billion pairs for 100,000 columns, rechecking the same runs from every start. Each column only needs to know where it is blocked on each side.

tests.note: flat wall: use the full width
rising: 3 x 3 = 9 beats the tallest column
the low middle column spans everything
tall thin column beats the long low strip
long low strip beats the tall column
equal heights next to each other

js: const stack = []; // indexes; heights increase from bottom to top
const h = i < heights.length ? heights[i] : 0; // a final 0 flushes the stack
// shorter neighbours: left is the new top, right is i
py: stack = []  # indexes; heights increase from bottom to top
h = heights[i] if i < len(heights) else 0  # a final 0 flushes the stack
# shorter neighbours: left is the new top, right is i
walkthrough: Try each column as "the shortest": its mural spreads sideways until a shorter column on each side. A stack of increasing heights finds both limits. When a shorter column arrives and pops a column, the newcomer is the popped column's right limit, and the column below it on the stack is its left limit.
• At i = 0 and i = 1 the heights 3 and 5 are increasing, so both are pushed. The stack is 0(3), 1(5).
• At i = 2 (height 4), the top has height 5, which is at least 4, so index 1 is popped with left 0, right 2, width 1 and area 5 × 1 = 5. Then 2 is pushed, and the stack is 0(3), 2(4).

• At i = 3 (height 1), index 2 is popped with left 0, width 3 - 0 - 1 = 2 and area 4 × 2 = 8. Index 0 is popped next; the stack is then empty, so left = -1, width 3 and area 3 × 3 = 9. Then 3 is pushed, and the stack is 3(1).
• At i = 4 (height 6), the height is larger than the top, so 4 is pushed. The stack is 3(1), 4(6).
• At i = 5 (height 2), index 4 is popped with left 3, width 1 and area 6. Then 5 is pushed, and the stack is 3(1), 5(2).
• At i = 6, the extra column of height 0, index 5 is popped with left 3, width 2 and area 4, and then index 3 is popped with left -1, width 6 and area 6.

The best area is 9. Two details matter. The final height-0 step flushes columns that never met a shorter one. And a popped column's area uses the index below it on the stack, not its own, because every column between them was taller and already popped.
solution.timeWhy: Each index is pushed once and popped once.
solution.spaceWhy: A rising wall keeps every index on the stack until the end.
solution.takeaway: When an element's answer depends on how far it stretches before hitting something smaller (or bigger), use a monotonic stack: when an element is popped, you know both its limits. This also solves the largest rectangle of 1s in a grid, one row at a time.
